what_happened: The user asked for something to be published. Athena read "publish" in its own way, and the user corrected that reading. The user said that publish means they can open the result at a URL, and that Athena should plan whatever jobs that takes. The first reading did not match that, so the output was corrected.
cause: Athena turns request wording into a reading without checking it against the outcome the user will observe. For verbs like publish, deploy or share, the real goal is a user-visible state, such as being reachable at a URL. Nothing requires a reading to be stated as an observable acceptance condition, so a narrow literal reading can pass unchallenged until the user corrects it.
prevention: Change reading generation so that every reading of a request is written as an observable outcome: what the user can do or see when the work is done. For delivery verbs such as publish, deploy, share or release, the reading must name the access point (URL, location, or recipient) and include every job needed to reach it, such as build, host and verify. Planning should not go ahead on a reading that only names an action with no checkable end state.
proposed_request: When interpreting a request, write each reading as an observable end state the user can check. For delivery verbs such as publish, deploy or share, the reading must state where the user will access the result, for example "I can open it at a URL". The plan must include all jobs needed to reach that state, including hosting and a check that the URL loads. Apply this to the current request, where publish means the user can open it at a URL.
